newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OFFICIAL DATA UNDERSTATES S.AFRICA JOBS -MINISTER.
newsitem.headline: OFFICIAL DATA UNDERSTATES S.AFRICA JOBS -MINISTER.

text.p: South Africa's employment position is considerably better than official figures suggest, trade and industry minister Alec Erwin said on Thursday.
"We believe the employment position is not being properly captured," he told parliament's finance committee.
The picture was being understated due to inadequate sampling which ignored many new municipal infrastructure jobs and over-emphasised the situation at established companies.

"Our assessment is that both last year and in 1995 there was a net increase in manufacturing employment. We take the view that the employment situation has not only stabilised but turned positive," he said.
Industry had adjusted surprisingly fast to reductions in tariffs which had reduced South Africa's trade weighted tariff level to 11 percent, the lowest of any southern African state, he added.
As a result, the clothing and textile sector -- one of the hardest hit by imported competiton -- was managing to create new jobs while the automobile industry had added 11,000 new posts in 1996.

Government would consult with industry on plans for compensatory changes in tariffs to take account of the fall in the rand in the last year, but Erwin said he was confident that manufacturers would also take these changes in their stride.
Erwin said projections given in the 1997/98 budget review were based on official statistics and gave a "worst case scenario" for the South African jobs market.
The budget review assumed non-agricultural employment growth of just 0.5 percent in the year to March 31, 1998, after a decline of 1.5 percent in 1996/97.
Official figures show formal employment has increased only once during any calendar year since 1989 when it rose by 0.7 percent in 1995.
